newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Ex-Nicaraguan rebels deny receiving drug money.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Nicaraguan rebels deny receiving drug money.

text.p: While U.S. officials investigate charges of CIA complicity in a drug-trafficking ring that financed Nicaraguan Contra rebels in the 1980s, former Contra commanders on Friday denied having received drug money.

"The charge is absurd. We never received a cent of drug money, and I don't believe U.S. government employees tried to finance us through drug trafficking," former Contra leader Adolfo Calero told Reuters at his home in Managua.

Calero, a member of the Contra high command during the war and head of the largest rebel faction, the Nicaraguan Democratic Force (FDN), called the allegations "a political ploy" to discredit the Republican Party in an election year.

Nicaragua's right-wing Contra rebels, funded by the United States and trained by the Central Intelligence Agency, fought an eight-year war against the Marxist Sandinista government in the 1980s that left 25,000 dead.

With U.S. support, they went from a ragtag band of supporters of former dictator Anastasio Somoza, who was toppled in the 1979 Sandinista revolution, into one of Latin America's largest guerrilla armies with 22,000 troops.
They disarmed in 1990, following the Sandinista's election loss to Violeta Chamorro.

Congress has investigated connections between the Contras and drug-trafficking since the mid-1980s, after President Ronald Reagan made toppling the Sandinistas a priority in his effort to stop communism in Central America.

An investigative report by the San Jose Mercury News in August alleged that a drug pipeline between Colombia and the San Francisco Bay area functioned for a decade with at least tacit CIA approval, funnelling millions in profits to the Contras.
The series also said the drug pipeline flooded Los Angeles with tons of crack cocaine, enraging U.S. black leaders who accused the CIA of sacrificing inner-city blacks.
The U.S. Justice Department said last week it was investigating the case.
Former Contra commander Luis Fley said the two drug dealers who allegedly ran the network, Norwin Meneses and Danilo Blandon, never belonged to the Contras.
"We would have beaten the Sandinista if we had been backed by drug traffickers," he said.
